The scene is a precise reply to their old game. In the world, they went back and forth between two groups and took the words that served each meeting. On that Day, they cannot cross the wall by changing speech. The side of the wall that holds grace is no longer gained through a claim. The same reply then names their past: they gave in to the test, waited for the believers to fall, doubted, and let false hopes fool them. This is why the response is not mere public shame. It unveils what their masks had hidden and sets each person with the side truly chosen. The mockers once treated faith as a role that could be put on. The Last Day shows that its light had to be received in the heart before that day came.

**RESPITE CAN BE A TEST RATHER THAN A SIGN OF APPROVAL**

The second part of the reply takes place even now. They are left time, and their revolt spreads within that time. The delay may look like success because no blow falls as soon as the lie is told. Yet lack of swift pain is not proof that God is pleased. Mercy may delay a due end so that a sinner can return. If he uses the delay to add pride to pride, the same span becomes a path toward a fuller account. The Qur’an warns of both the slow approach and the perfect plan: (7:182 — **“As for those who deny Our signs, We will gradually draw them to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend”**), followed by (7:183 — **“I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”**).

This does not make sin grow without a first choice. The passage has already shown lies, scorn, and willful ties with evil chiefs. The added room meets a revolt they keep choosing. Another verse says of those fixed in disbelief, (3:178 — **“They are only given more time to increase in sin, and they will suffer a humiliating punishment”**). Thus, divine patience must not be read through results alone. Wealth, access, praise, and freedom from an immediate cost may all remain while a person moves farther from truth. The true use of respite is repentance. Each quiet day is time to drop the mask, repair a wrong, and seek light. To spend it on new fraud is to turn a gift of time into proof against oneself.

**BLIND MOTION IS NOT THE SAME AS A GUIDED PATH**

Their defiance crosses set bounds, while their blind wandering keeps them from a clear end. They are active, but activity is not guidance. A lost traveller may move fast and still add mile after mile to the wrong road. Speed then makes the error grow more quickly. In the same way, the hypocrites plan, meet, speak, and gain, yet none of that motion gives them a sound aim. Their confusion is moral, not a slur against people who lack physical sight. It lies in the will that refused the first light. The order is stated elsewhere: (6:110 — **“We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first,”**). Refusal comes first; being left to roam follows as judgment.

The warning is close today because quick success can look like a verdict from God. A lie may win the room. Mockery may earn laughs. A double pledge may keep two sets of friends. This verse says that none of those results can prove the road is safe. The right questions concern truth, God’s bounds, and the end toward which each choice moves the heart. A believer should not ask to be led on in a wrong that feels easy. He asks to be corrected while correction still hurts, to see the harm beneath a short gain, and to use every delay as a door back. The worst answer to mockery is not that the mocker fails at once. It is that he is allowed to think he won until his blindness has carried him far from home.

---

## Verse 2:16

> They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided

**THE VERDICT GATHERS THE WHOLE PATTERN INTO ONE CHOICE**

After the claims, lies, scorn, and blind wandering, the words ***“They are the ones”*** gather the traits into a single account. These are not stray faults that happen to sit beside one another. Each one serves the same hidden choice. They speak faith to gain trust, return to their chiefs to guard their place, and call the faithful foolish so that true guidance will seem unworthy of its cost. The verse now reads that course as a bargain. This matters because a bargain joins desire, judgment, and action. A buyer sees two things, values one above the other, and gives something up to gain what he wants. The hypocrites are not mere victims of a fog they did not choose. They have seen enough of both paths to prefer the one that grants a quick worldly edge. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd describe them as pursuing error and leaving guidance, while Qatādah stresses their preference for the wrong path. Their many acts are thus traced to a rule within: when truth and near gain part ways, they keep the gain.

**A PRICELESS GOOD IS HANDED OVER FOR ERROR**

They are those ***“who trade guidance for misguidance.”*** The image does not require that every hypocrite first possessed full, settled faith and then sold it. Mujāhid applied it to people who believed and then disbelieved. The wider reading includes those to whom guidance came, who knew its call and could have received it, but chose its opposite. This is why preference itself can be pictured as exchange. An earlier people were shown the way, (41:17 — **“but they preferred blindness over guidance. So the blast of a disgracing punishment overtook them”**). Access to light made their chosen blindness blameworthy. The price and the goods are reversed. Guidance is what should have been sought, while error is what should have been cast away. Instead, they spend the better thing to obtain the worse. Their worldly plan may bring safety, praise from chiefs, or a share in two circles, but none of those gains equals what is lost. The Qur’an uses the same market image for people who (2:86 — **“trade the Hereafter for the life of this world. So their punishment will not be reduced,”**). The fault is not trade itself. Lawful trade can be part of seeking God’s bounty. The fault is using a trader’s care for gain while leaving the final account out of the price. A sound bargain guards what lasts; this bargain spends it.

**THEIR LEDGER SHOWS ACTIVITY BUT NO PROFIT**

The result follows at once: ***“But this trade is profitless”***. Profit is what remains after cost is counted, not whatever enters the hand first. The hypocrites count shelter, rank, and access, but omit the split heart, the growing lie, the loss of light, and the judgment to come. Once all costs are entered, the supposed gain disappears. Their case is like a merchant who celebrates the coins in his till while ignoring that he sold the whole shop to get them. Much moved through his hands, yet he ended with less than he began. This verdict also explains why a scheme may appear to work and still fail. They may fool a person for a day. That result does not turn fraud into profit, because the deepest object of the plan was safety and well-being for the self. Verse 9 has already shown that they deceive only themselves. A later line repeats the same exchange with its end in view: (2:175 — **“They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment.”**). What they gain cannot shield them from what they bought. By contrast, God describes a true exchange in which believers give life and wealth for Paradise, then says, (9:111 — **“So rejoice in the exchange you have made with Him. That is ˹truly˺ the ultimate triumph”**). The worth of a trade is known by its seller, price, object, and final delivery. On every count, the hypocrites’ trade loses.

**THE UNGUIDED CHOICE AND THE ROAD AFTER IT**

The close says ***“and they are not ˹rightly˺ guided”***. They lacked sound judgment in the exchange, and they do not reach a safe road after it. This ending ties the market image back to travel. A bad bargain leaves one poor; rejected guidance also leaves one lost. Their clever speech cannot make up for the lack of a true end. They know how to move between groups, but not how to move toward God. They know which claim may please each room, but not which choice will stand on the Last Day. Today, people still trade in things that have no price tag. A person may give up truth for access, prayer for praise, trust for a short advantage, or conscience for a place near power. The payment may be hidden because no money changes hands. Yet a real exchange has occurred. The warning demands a full account before such a choice is made. The rightly guided are (39:18 — **“those who listen to what is said and follow the best of it. These are the ones ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah,”**). They do not ask only what a choice gains now, but what it does to faith and where it leads. Guidance is kept by acting on its worth. Once it is treated as expendable, even a crowded ledger can close with nothing but loss.

---

## Verse 2:17

> Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see

**THE INNER CONDITION IS TURNED INTO A SCENE**

The account now shifts from direct charge to a picture: ***“Their example is that of someone”***. A parable lets the hearer see in one moment what the prior verses traced through many acts. There is night, a needed flame, a brief ring of sight, and then a loss more stark because light came first. The single figure can stand for the whole group, much as one scene can show the shared state of many people. Their details may differ, but the pattern is one: they approach the signs of faith, gain from being near them, and fail to receive the light as an inward guide. The parable does not ask the reader to match each speck of the scene to a separate event. Its main force lies in the movement from need to light and from light to chosen loss. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the worldly side through the safety their public claim gave to person, family, and wealth. Ibn ʿAbbās also places the full loss at death, when an outward claim can no longer supply what only true faith gives. Both stages expose the same flaw. They used the setting of light without making its truth their own.

**A FIRE GIVES REAL HELP FOR A SHORT TIME**

The figure is one ***“who kindles a fire”***. He does so in darkness because fire can show danger, mark a path, give warmth, and calm fear. In the same way, the rise of faith around the hypocrites brings real signs and real worldly goods. They hear the Qur’an, see the Prophet’s life, join the Muslim group, and receive the public rights tied to their claim. The light around them is not false merely because their use of it is false. This point keeps the parable from becoming a claim that they met no guidance at all. They came close enough to see for a time, but treated what they saw as a tool for safety rather than a truth to obey.

There is also a difference between being lit from within and standing for a while in light made by another. Early explanation notes that the flame was obtained for a need, not held as a secure source within the man himself. That detail suits a borrowed profession of faith. Words and company can place someone near the effects of belief, yet neither can replace trust in the heart. The Qur’an describes a sounder gift as life joined to (6:122 — **“a light with which they can walk among people”**). Such light directs steps because God has given life to the person who bears it. The hypocrites seek the shelter of the lit circle while refusing the bond that would let them walk by its truth.

**THE USEFUL LIGHT GOES WHILE THE HARM REMAINS**

The turn comes ***“but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness”***. The timing sharpens the loss. They have seen enough to know what light does; then the good they tried to borrow is gone. The sentence begins with one fire-maker and turns to the group whose state he pictures. This prevents the reader from losing the hypocrites inside the image. God is the One who removes the light, just as He had left them to range in revolt after their own repeated refusal. The wording names the light as what is taken. Early readers drew from this that the useful part is lost while the painful result remains. Fire can shine and burn; they sought its shelter but end with no light to guide them. Doubt, disbelief, fear, and the cost of deceit now close in. This is just because they did not lose a sincere faith against their will. They kept rejecting the purpose of the light while trying to retain its side benefits. The Last Day will make the difference plain. Believing men and women will have (57:12 — **“their light shining ahead of them and on their right”**), while a borrowed public place will not produce that light. What survives then is what faith formed, not what a mask once gained.

**NO SIGHT REMAINS FOR THE WAY OUT**

The last words are ***“unable to see”***. Ordinary eyes are not the issue. The figure cannot find his road when the flame dies, and the people pictured cannot find guidance while they guard the cause of their dark state. Another parable describes deeds beneath waves and clouds as (24:40 — **“Darkness upon darkness! If one stretches out their hand, they can hardly see it.”**). Layers make the loss worse: doubt clouds truth, lies guard the doubt, mockery resists advice, and evil company praises the whole course. Each layer makes return seem less needful. The image is therefore a warning against living on light that belongs only to one’s setting. Today, a person may grow up near scripture, use the speech of faith, and enjoy trust among believers while the heart avoids surrender. Nearness is a gift, but it is not a substitute for response. The right answer is not fear without hope. Believers themselves are told to repent and ask, (66:8 — **“Perfect our light for us, and forgive us. ˹For˺ You are truly Most Capable of everything.””**). Light is kept through sincere faith, pardon, and steps taken by it. The parable urges the reader to receive the truth before familiar words become a mere glow around a heart that still chooses night.

---

## Verse 2:18

> They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺

**THEY HAVE ORGANS OF SENSE BUT REFUSE THEIR MORAL USE**

The brief verdict completes the fire scene: ***“They are ˹wilfully˺ deaf, dumb”***. The translation’s added wilfully keeps the image tied to choice. These people heard the Qur’an, spoke claims of faith, and watched the believers whom they mocked. Their bodies could receive sound and form words. What failed was the use of those gifts for truth. Ibn ʿAbbās says they behaved as though deaf, mute, and blind. They made themselves unresponsive when guidance called, though they stayed keenly alert to rank, fear, and gain. This is why another verse joins the same two traits to a lack of understanding: (8:22 — **“the ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb, who do not understand”**). Hearing in the moral sense is more than sound reaching the ear. It includes attention, recognition, and a will to answer. A warning that causes no honest thought has not been heard in the way revelation seeks. The fault lies not in a limit of the body but in a heart that trains the body’s powers to serve every aim except truth.

**A TONGUE FULL OF CLAIMS CAN STILL BE DUMB TO GOOD**

Their muteness may seem strange after so many verses record their speech. They say they believe, call themselves reformers, insult the faithful, assure their chiefs, and boast of mockery. The very amount of speech proves that physical silence is not meant. They are mute toward the good word that would make speech true: open faith, confession of wrong, sound counsel, and praise of the truth they know. Speech does not fulfil its gift merely by being clever or abundant. It fulfils it when the tongue bears witness to what is right and binds the speaker to it. The contrast with faith appears in a simple response. When true believers are called to God and His Messenger for judgment, their answer (24:51 — **“is to say, “We hear and obey.” It is they who will ˹truly˺ succeed”**). Hearing becomes speech, and speech opens into action. The hypocrites break that chain at each point. They hear but do not yield, speak but do not tell the inward truth, and act without the loyalty their words claim. Ibn ʿAbbās’s description of their pretended muteness therefore reaches the core: they have words for disguise but none for return. The verse does not belittle anyone who cannot speak. A person without a voice may bear the clearest witness through faith and deed. The blame falls on those who possess a way to affirm truth and choose to use it against truth.

**BLINDNESS HERE BELONGS TO THE HEART’S JUDGMENT**

The description continues ***“and blind, so they will never return ˹to the Right Path˺”***. Verse 17 left the people in darkness; this verse shows that their long refusal has also spoiled the sight by which a path is known. The Qur’an states the difference from bodily blindness without any doubt: (22:46 — **“it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts in the chests that grow blind”**). Their eyes can note which group is strong and where a worldly chance lies. They fail to see the worth of guidance, the ugliness of deceit, and the end toward which their choices lead. The three lost powers form a full account of failed response. The ear does not receive, the tongue does not confess, and the eye does not find the road. Knowledge can still sit in memory while bringing no benefit. Earlier peoples were given hearing, sight, and minds, (46:26 — **“But neither their hearing, sight, nor intellect were of any benefit to them whatsoever,”**) because they kept denying the signs. Gifts become proof against the person when their true use is refused. They are like clear windows that have been painted over from within: daylight remains outside, but the chosen layer blocks its help. Each fresh coat makes the room darker and makes the darkness feel more normal.

**RETURN REQUIRES AN OPENING THEY KEEP SHUT**

The closing result is not a claim that repentance has no value or that a living reader should despair after sin. It describes the people in the parable as they persist in the condition God has exposed. They do not return because they have disabled every route by which correction would be welcomed. Advice is not heard, truth is not owned aloud, and the safe road is not seen as safe. The earlier verses also gave the order: they chose error, mocked faith, and were then left to wander. Judgment meets a will that keeps shutting the door. For the reader today, the opposite path is concrete. One listens long enough for a hard truth to reach the heart. One says what is true even when the old mask loses value. One looks beyond the nearest gain to the road and its end. Revelation remains (50:37 — **“a reminder for whoever has a ˹mindful˺ heart and lends an attentive ear”**). An attentive ear is still an opening. The verse warns against closing it by habit, not against seeking help for a bodily limit. Faith can be whole in a person who cannot hear, speak, or see; it is gravely broken in one who has all three powers but turns each away from God.

---

## Verse 2:19

> Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺

**A SECOND PARABLE SHOWS FEAR WITHIN THE GIFT**

The first picture ended with a dead fire. The next begins with water from above: ***“Or ˹those caught in˺ a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder”***. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Mujāhid, and Qatādah all understood the central image as pouring rain. Rain gives life, yet a person caught in a night storm may notice danger before benefit. This tension makes the scene fit people who come near revelation but meet it with divided hearts. The Qur’an descends as guidance and mercy, while its commands, warnings, and demands expose what they wish to keep safe. They want whatever shelter faith may give without yielding to the Lord who sends it. The parable does not call revelation dark or harmful. The storm contains water and light; the darkness belongs to their doubt and the fear with which they face what should revive them. In the created world, lightning itself can awaken both hope and fear, and God is the One who (13:12 — **“shows you lightning, inspiring ˹you with˺ hope and fear, and produces heavy clouds”**). A sound heart receives both sides and still sees the Giver. Their hearts treat every grave sign as a threat to escape. This is why the benefit can be present while their response remains ruled by fear.

**THREE SIGNS MEET A DIVIDED HEART**

The storm holds three features at once: ***“and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the darkness as the trials and confusion disclosed in the Qur’an, the thunder as its rebuke and threats, and the lightning as its clear teaching and promise. Other early readings likewise connect darkness with doubt and hypocrisy. These links do not remove the force of the real storm. They let its mixed force show a mixed response. Light draws the eye, thunder shakes the heart, and darkness makes each next step unsure. The fingers in the ears reveal which part they most want to stop. They do not wait, listen, and learn whether the sound marks danger or brings needed rain. They try to shut out the warning itself. The wording pictures the whole finger thrust in, though only its tip can enter, which makes the panic vivid. Yet blocking the ear does not still the sky. In the same way, refusing a recited warning cannot cancel what it warns about. The hypocrites hope that unheard truth will lose its claim on them. The effect is less readiness for the danger and less ability to receive the mercy carried in the same revelation.

**FEAR OF DEATH MAKES THEM CHOOSE A DEADLIER SHELTER**

Their frantic act is ***“for fear of death.”*** On the surface, a violent thunderclap can make a traveller fear that the storm will kill him. Within the parable, the warning of judgment and the cost of sincere faith feel like threats to the life the hypocrites have built. Ibn ʿAbbās says they feared being drawn to the Qur’an, for true response would end the false stance by which they served both sides. They also feared the punishments announced to disbelief, but sought relief by stopping the message rather than stopping its cause. Fear thus turns against its proper work. It should move a person away from ruin; theirs moves them away from the warning that marks ruin. No hand over an ear can bar death. The direct reminder is, (62:8 — **“The death you are running away from will inevitably come to you.”**). Nor can fear justify the lie that makes the final meeting worse. A believer also fears judgment, but joins fear to hope and action. He listens, seeks pardon, and changes course. The hypocrite uses fear to protect the course itself. This difference matters today when a person avoids a verse, adviser, or fact because it threatens comfort. Relief gained by not listening is not safety. The reason is that a warning guards a person only when it is heard and allowed to guide. Ignoring it may mean losing the last clear alarm before harm.

**NO SHELTER FALLS OUTSIDE DIVINE POWER**

The scene closes by moving from their hands to divine power: ***“And Allah encompasses the disbelievers ˹by His might˺”***. Ibn ʿAbbās joins God’s full knowledge to the certainty that He will gather them for judgment. To encompass is more than to stand near. No route falls outside His knowledge, no shelter resists His power, and no hidden fear or plan slips beyond His account. The storm may seem to close around the travellers, but God already holds both the storm and those within it. This ending also corrects the instinct behind their act. They behave as though danger lies in the sound and safety lies in a small wall made by their own fingers. The true issue is their bond with God. Another concise verse states, (85:20 — **“But Allah encompasses them from all sides”**). Flight within His creation cannot become flight from Him. Therefore, the sound response is not to silence warning but to seek the mercy to which warning points. When revelation brings promise and threat together, faith does not tear them apart. It lets promise guard against despair and threat guard against ease in sin. The hypocrite hears only what endangers his mask; the believer hears a Lord who sends rain, light, warning, and a road through the storm.

---

## Verse 2:20

> It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything

**A FLASH CAN DAZZLE WITHOUT BECOMING A STEADY GUIDE**

The storm reaches the eye: ***“It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight.”*** A near strike floods the dark with such force that the traveller is dazzled by the very thing that lets him see. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the flash as the Qur’an’s clear disclosure, which comes close to tearing away their error. The image holds both clarity and danger because their hearts do not receive clarity in a sound way. Proof breaks through, yet pride and doubt make its arrival feel like an attack. The words say that sight is almost taken, not that it has already gone. They still have moments in which a road appears and response remains possible. This makes their next act more revealing. They are not people to whom no light ever came; they are people whose use of light changes with the ease it offers. After describing rain and hail, another verse says, (24:43 — **“The flash of the clouds’ lightning nearly takes away eyesight”**). Here that created fact gives the parable its force while clear revelation exposes what their divided will does with a moment of sight.

**THEY MOVE ONLY WHILE FAITH SERVES THE NEAR MOMENT**

Their unstable course appears in ***“Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light”***. The flash is enough for a few steps, but they do not commit themselves to the road or to the One who shows it. Early readers connect this movement to the truths, gains, and ease in faith that suit them. When public belief gives safety or the believers gain strength, the hypocrites move among them. A later description catches the same wait for advantage: (4:141 — **“˹The hypocrites are˺ those who wait to see what happens to you. So if Allah grants you victory, they say ˹to you˺,”**). Their allegiance follows the visible turn rather than guiding them through it. This is not a rebuke of every pause in confusion. A sincere believer may stop to learn, seek proof, or avoid a rash act. The difference is that sincere caution wants enough light to obey, while hypocrisy wants only enough light to gain. Its standard shifts with comfort. The Qur’an depicts another person who worships at the edge: (22:11 — **“if they are afflicted with a trial, they relapse ˹into disbelief˺, losing this world and the Hereafter.”**). Faith rooted in God can walk through a hard command because truth remains true when the weather changes. Faith used as a bargain moves only while the next patch of ground looks useful.

**DARKNESS EXPOSES THE LACK OF AN INNER COURSE**

The other half follows: ***“but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing”***. The sudden stop is more than sensible shelter from a storm. Within the parable, doubt and disliked duties leave them with no settled aim of their own. They cannot move by trust when a quick worldly benefit is no longer visible. This is why their stillness belongs with the motion before it. Both are ruled by the same demand for immediate gain. The effect is a life of reaction: advance when success shines, freeze when cost appears, and never choose the road for its true end. The mention of hearing returns to the fingers pressed into ears in verse 19. They act as though hearing belongs to them to block at will, but God can remove the gift itself. The warning also joins moral loss to bodily power without confusing the two. Their inward hearing has failed through refusal; their outward hearing remains under the Lord who gave it. God asks elsewhere, (6:46 — **“Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who”**) other than Him could restore it. A faculty is not secure merely because it works today. Its right response is gratitude and use in the service of truth.

**SIGHT, SOUND, AND EVERY OUTCOME REST IN DIVINE POWER**

The close completes the threat: ***“and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything”***. Hearing and sight are named because the storm has tested both. Thunder met the ear, lightning met the eye, and the hypocrites misused each meeting. The final statement widens the view beyond the storm. God can preserve, remove, judge, guide, and bring every promised end. No part of the parable lies outside His rule, and no clever shift between light and dark limits what He can do. This power should awaken thanks as well as fear. Humanity is reminded, (67:23 — **“He is the One Who brought you into being and gave you hearing, sight, and intellect.”**). Thanks is not only spoken praise. It is to let the ear receive what is true and the eye read signs as signs. Today, a person may obey while faith brings social ease, then stop when it costs status, time, or desire. The changing cost does not change the Lord or the road. Steady faith stores the direction given in light and follows it when the next stretch is hard. The storm parable warns against making convenience the lamp, because convenience flashes and fades. God’s guidance, received with a whole heart, supplies a course beyond the next bright moment.

---

## Verse 2:21

> O humanity! Worship your Lord, Who created you and those before you, so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺

**AFTER THREE PORTRAITS, THE CALL OPENS TO EVERY PERSON**

The surah has shown the faithful, open rejecters, and hypocrites. It now turns from describing them to addressing all: ***“O humanity! Worship your Lord”***. No group can treat the command as meant only for the others. Believers hear the duty to remain true and deepen obedience. Open rejecters are called away from denial. Hypocrites are offered the direct cure for divided speech: serve one Lord with an undivided heart. Ibn ʿAbbās applied the first hearing to the people of Makkah, and another early application included Jews who heard the call. Yet the form reaches humanity, not one tribe, class, or age. This is why the shift matters. The differences just described are moral responses, not separate kinds of human worth that bar anyone from the command. All stand as servants before the same Lord. Another universal address begins from the same bond: (4:1 — **“O humanity! Be mindful of your Lord Who created you from a single soul, and from it He created its mate,”**). Shared origin supports shared duty and leaves no ground for pride before the Creator.

**THE LORD WHO NURTURES ALONE DESERVES WORSHIP**

The command names Him as their Lord, the One who creates, owns, sustains, and brings His servants through every stage. Worship is therefore not a gift offered to meet a need in God. He needs no food or aid: (51:57 — **“I seek no provision from them, nor do I need them to feed Me”**). He is the Provider, while the servants are the ones upheld. Worship answers the truth of that relation. It declares His oneness, bows to His command, trusts His report, loves what He loves, and refuses rivals in the right that belongs to Him alone. Ibn ʿAbbās places the oneness of God at the heart of the command. Early explanation also gathers worship into obeying commands, avoiding bans, and accepting what God has made known. Prayer, remembrance, and sacrifice are clear acts of worship, but they train a wider life. Honest trade, care for parents, restraint from wrong, and patient service become worship when they follow God’s rule and seek His pleasure. This breadth keeps worship from being reduced to a set of motions cut off from character. It also keeps ordinary good deeds from becoming self-made religion, since the Lord who gives life also teaches how it should be lived. Humanity was not made because God lacked servants; the purpose belongs to human need and divine wisdom: (51:56 — **“I did not create jinn and humans except to worship Me”**).

**CREATION IS THE PROOF PLACED BESIDE THE COMMAND**

The One addressed is He ***“Who created you and those before you”***. The proof is closer than a distant sign. Each hearer exists without having designed, willed, or brought himself from nothing. The same is true of parents, rulers, heroes, and every past people. Going back through the line never reaches a human being who created the whole chain. This is why creation grounds worship. The giver of existence has a claim no creature can share, and the One who began life is able to direct its proper end. Another verse joins the two without a gap: (6:102 — **“˹He is˺ the Creator of all things, so worship Him ˹alone˺. And He is the Maintainer of everything”**). The mention of those before us also cuts two false claims. Tradition cannot make a rival worthy of worship merely because ancestors served it, and ancestry cannot make one group self-sufficient before God. Those before were created servants just as those alive now are. Their lives can teach, but they cannot replace the Creator’s right. At the same time, the line gives comfort. The Lord’s care did not begin with the present crisis or the present generation. He brought countless people through birth, provision, duty, and death before us. Worship places a short human life within that larger truth rather than leaving it to invent its own centre.

**MINDFULNESS IS THE FRUIT TOWARD WHICH WORSHIP TRAINS THE HEART**

The aim is ***“so that you may become mindful ˹of Him˺”***. This wording does not express doubt in God’s knowledge or an anxious hope about what He cannot control. It sets before the hearers the outcome they should seek: worship your Lord so that a guarded, God-aware life may grow. Mindfulness watches the boundary before crossing it. It remembers the One who sees when no person is present, and it keeps fear joined to love and hope. Ibn ʿAbbās connects the result to guarding oneself from divine anger through obedience. The link is not mechanical. An outward act can be emptied by display, as the account of hypocrites has shown. Worship forms mindfulness when the servant knows whom he serves and carries that bond beyond the act. Prayer renews account, fasting trains restraint, charity loosens greed, and remembrance interrupts heedlessness. The command to believers is therefore, (3:102 — **“Be mindful of Allah in the way He deserves, and do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission ˹to Him˺”**). Today, this verse asks more than whether worship appears in a schedule. It asks whether worship makes choice, speech, money, desire, and hidden life more aware of God. The Lord created every part of life; true service returns every part to His guidance.

---

## Verse 2:22

> ˹He is the One˺ Who has made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy; and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow as a provision for you. So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺

**DAILY LIFE RESTS ON GIFTS NO HUMAN MADE**

The description continues without changing its subject: ***“˹He is the One˺”***. The Lord whom humanity must worship is now known through gifts used every day. This keeps worship tied to both origin and care. God did not create and abandon His creatures; He ordered a world in which they can rest, build, drink, plant, and eat. The repeated address to you turns vast signs into personal trust. Earth and sky are not remote ideas. Each breath, step, roof, crop, and meal depends on an order no human being began. Ibn ʿAbbās reads these gifts as provision not only for the hearers but for created beings around them. The point is therefore larger than bare survival. A world fitted for life displays care, and care deepens the claim already grounded in creation. This is why the command against rivals comes after the list. Gratitude that stops at the gift or at a created means has not yet reached the Giver.

**THE GROUND IS SETTLED AND THE SKY RISES ABOVE IT**

God is the One ***“Who has made the earth a place of settlement”***, ***“for you and the sky a canopy”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the first image through dwelling and rest. The earth is firm enough for ordinary life, broad enough for travel, and fit for farms, homes, and paths. Calling it a settled place speaks from the true scale of human use; it is not a claim that every patch is soft, safe, or easy. Mountains, deserts, seas, and quakes remain part of the created world, while humanity as a whole receives ground on which life can be established. The canopy image turns the gaze upward. The sky covers the human dwelling and holds signs and benefits that life needs. The pairing returns in another description: (40:64 — **“It is Allah Who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy.”**). The sky is also called (21:32 — **“a well-protected canopy, still they turn away from its signs”**). The rebuke there shows that protection should lead to recognition. Yet neither earth nor sky is divine. Both are made arrangements serving a purpose set by their Lord. This distinction guards thought from two errors: ignoring the created order as though it had no Giver, and worshipping a part of that order because its scale inspires awe. The earth bears us and the sky covers us, but neither chose its task or owns the one who benefits.

**WATER LINKS HEAVEN, SOIL, PLANT, AND DAILY BREAD**

The next gift moves through a chain described as ***“and sends down rain from the sky, causing fruits to grow”***, giving it ***“as a provision for you.”*** Rain descends, soil receives it, seed opens, and produce forms in kinds, colours, and tastes. The brief line gathers stages that no farmer can create from nothing. Human labour is real: people clear, sow, water, guard, harvest, carry, and sell. Yet effort works only with water, life, matter, time, and stable laws already given. The verse therefore does not erase created causes. It places them under the One who gives each cause its power and joins them to their fruit. The Qur’an draws attention to the range within this gift: (16:11 — **“With it He produces for you ˹various˺ crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit.”**). Variety serves body, trade, pleasure, and thought. Provision is thus more than ownership. It is a trust whose source should shape its use. Gratitude does not permit waste, fraud, or the hoarding of food while others are wronged. It receives, shares, and obeys the Provider. Today, knowledge of clouds, roots, and growth can deepen this response rather than displace it. Explaining a stage in the chain does not explain away the existence of the chain, its powers, or the Lord who sustains them.

**KNOWN CREATION MAKES RIVALS AN OPEN CONTRADICTION**

The conclusion follows: ***“So do not knowingly set up equals to Allah ˹in worship˺”***. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the rivals as peers or equals assigned to God. The final knowingly points to what the hearers already admit or can plainly infer: they did not create earth, raise the sky, send rain, or originate the life in fruit. Other passages confront people who confess that God created heaven and earth and sent rain, yet fail to give Him the worship due to that knowledge. When asked who sends rain and revives dead soil, (29:63 — **“they will surely say, “Allah!” Say, “Praise be to Allah!” In fact, most of them do not understand”**). The missing step is not a new fact about rain. It is faithful action on what they know.

A rival is not every tool, leader, or person from whom help is sought. Created means can be used while the heart knows their limits and obeys God. Rivalry begins when a creature receives a share of worship, ultimate reliance, sacred obedience against God, or the fear and love that belong to Him alone. The reason is direct: the One alone creates and provides, so He alone deserves worship. This truth frees the servant as well as binding him. Work, medicine, wealth, and power may be used, but none becomes a lord. Their benefit remains granted, bounded, and removable. Knowledge becomes whole when the hand takes lawful means while the heart bows only to the One who made them. That order preserves both effort and trust.

---

## Verse 2:23

> And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true

**DOUBT IS CALLED OUT OF VAGUENESS INTO A TEST**

After signs of the Creator, the surah turns to the source of the Book itself: ***“And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant”***. The doubt at issue concerns whether the Qur’an truly comes from God. The speakers who claimed that the Prophet made it had heard its recitation and knew the man through whom it came. Rather than asking them to silence the claim by force, revelation puts a test beside it. This matters because a charge of human authorship has a result that can be examined: if one man made this discourse, other able speakers should be able to meet its kind. The verse therefore moves the dispute from vague dislike to a stated task. Honest questions are not condemned merely for arising; they are required to follow evidence and accept what the test shows. Another passage invites reflection on the Book’s unity: (4:82 — **“Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have certainly found in it many inconsistencies”**). Doubt must do the work it claims to demand, not remain a shelter from every answer.

**REVELATION COMES FROM ABOVE TO A HUMAN SERVANT**

The wording places two roles in clear order. God says that He revealed, while Muḥammad is honoured as His servant. Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the servant here with the Prophet whom the opponents charged with fabrication. Servanthood does not lessen the Messenger; it locates his greatness in faithful reception and delivery. He is neither the Qur’an’s source nor a partner in God’s speech. He receives, recites, teaches, and obeys what comes down. This also keeps the proof from resting on a claim that he was more than human. The challenge works precisely because a human messenger stands among people who know human speech. His known life forms part of the setting. Before revelation he had not read prior writings or produced a written book, as the Qur’an reminds its opponents: (29:48 — **“You ˹O Prophet˺ could not read any writing ˹even˺ before this ˹revelation˺, nor could you write at all.”**). Then a sustained recitation came through him with its own voice, law, stories, warnings, prayers, and vision of God and the world. The claim made by the verse is not that its words merely inspired his thought. The descent is from God to His servant. This is why the proper question concerns whether the recited Book can be explained as the servant’s invention.

**ONE SŪRAH IS ENOUGH FOR THE CHALLENGE**

The demand is direct: ***“then produce a sûrah like it”***. The opponents need not reproduce the whole Qur’an. The challenge narrows the task to one bounded passage while keeping the demand for likeness. Early explanation points to its eloquence, ordered form, and knowledge as parts of what must be faced. Its force is not captured by choosing one pleasing line or copying a rhyme. A true answer would need to stand as discourse of the same kind, joining wording, meaning, form, truth, and guidance rather than imitating a surface feature. The claim of fabrication is thus tested on the ground chosen by the accusers themselves: human speech. The challenge appears in several forms across the Qur’an. One passage asks, (11:13 — **“Produce ten fabricated sûrahs like it and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!””**). Another repeats the demand for one: (10:38 — **“Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!””**). The broadest form brings humans and jinn together, then states, (17:88 — **“they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other.””**). These are not rival tests. They close routes of excuse: whole or part, lone effort or joined force, the claim remains unmet. Since the Qur’an declares itself (26:195 — **“in a clear Arabic tongue”**), its full verbal challenge concerns the Arabic recitation, not an English rendering. A translation can carry meaning and open study, but it does not replace the form in which the challenge was first heard.

**ALL HELP IS ALLOWED, SO THE CLAIM MUST FACE ITS OWN RESULT**

The next permission is wide: ***“and call your helpers other than Allah”***. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the helpers as aids and also relates the phrase to the gods the challengers served. A report transmitted by al-Suddī includes partners and other people; Mujāhid points to skilled speakers who might support the claim. The range strengthens the test. Pride cannot answer that one person lacked time or skill. Let allies, patrons, critics, and every power invoked besides God join the effort. The only excluded help is the very source they deny, for receiving another revelation from God would concede the point. The condition is ***“if what you say is true”***. Truthfulness here is more than confidence. A claim that carries grave moral weight must bear proof and submit to a fair result. Today, readers should not reduce this verse to a slogan used without study. Its challenge invites close attention to language, structure, message, coherence, setting, and the Prophet’s life. Nor should a Muslim fear careful examination, since the verse itself directs doubt toward a public test. The right posture joins intellectual honesty to moral honesty: define the claim, use the allowed evidence, and do not move the standard merely because the answer costs pride. The next verse will state the result of the challenge and the consequence of refusing what that result shows.

---

## Verse 2:24

> But if you are unable to do so—and you will never be able to do so—then fear the Fire fuelled with people and stones, which is prepared for the disbelievers

**THE TEST IS ALLOWED TO REACH ITS RESULT**

The challenge now passes from proposal to outcome: ***“But if you are unable to do”*** what was asked, the claim of human authorship has failed its own test. The point is that the invited test now bears on the moral right to keep denying. The conditional form gives the opponents room to try; it does not imply that God lacks knowledge of the result. They may gather helpers, use their skill, and bring forward whatever they think meets the demand. Failure after that open permission is evidence, not mere silence imposed by authority. Early explanation stresses that the challengers and their allies had been allowed to spend their effort before their lack of power was laid bare. This is why the next command carries moral weight. Once a fair test defeats the excuse, keeping the old charge is no longer a neutral pause. It is refusal of what the result shows. A similar challenge says, (52:34 — **“Let them then produce something like it, if what they say is true”**). Truthfulness requires accepting not only a desired result but also the result that overturns one’s claim.

**THE FUTURE IS STATED BEFORE THE CENTURIES UNFOLD**

The sentence interrupts the condition with certainty: ***“so and you will never be able to do”*** it. Qatādah reads this as a lack of power to meet the challenge, while Ibn ʿAbbās says that any attempt will fail. The statement looks forward beyond the first hearers. It is not merely a report that no rival passage had appeared by that day; it declares that the failure will continue. The Qur’an therefore places its claim where later enemies, skilled speakers, and whole groups can confront it. This is why the opening if does not express doubt in God. Human hearers must discover their inability through the offered test, while God announces what their trial will show. The two parts belong together: try if the charge is true, but know that created speech will not become the speech of its Creator. This does not make every imitation worthless as human writing. People can copy sounds, borrow themes, or compose eloquent lines. The test concerns producing a sūrah of its kind, with the joined force named in the prior verse. Surface likeness cannot erase the deeper failure any more than painting a flame can supply heat.

**FEAR BECOMES A COMMAND TO SEEK SAFETY**

The answer is not to invent a new excuse but ***“so then fear the Fire fuelled with people”***. The call to fear is a call to guard oneself through belief, worship, and a changed course. It does not tell the hearer to stare at punishment without hope. The warning comes while response is possible, which means that its purpose is rescue. The same direct command appears elsewhere: (3:131 — **“Guard yourselves against the Fire prepared for the disbelievers”**). Fear serves mercy when it moves the person away from the cause of harm. The fuel makes the warning personal. In an earthly fire, people stand outside and add wood. Here unrepentant rejecters do not control the flame; they become part of what it consumes. The image ends any thought that the debate concerns words alone. Calling revelation false after its proof has been faced shapes a person’s bond with God and final end. Yet no reader may take this as leave to assign named living people to the Fire. Revelation states the fate of disbelief and identifies the people addressed by God’s knowledge. Human duty is to convey, warn, pray for guidance, and judge outward matters with justice.

**STONES EXPOSE THE POWERLESSNESS OF EVERY FALSE GOD**

The description continues with ***“and stones, which is prepared”*** ***“for the disbelievers”***. Ibn ʿAbbās understood the stones as sulphur, which stresses the terror and heat of the fuel. Another early reading sees the idols that people carved and worshipped. The Qur’an supports that humiliation of false gods: (21:98 — **“Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell.”**). It then says, (21:99 — **“Had those idols been ˹true˺ gods, they would not have entered it.”**). What was treated as a source of aid cannot save itself, much less its worshipper. The wording says that the Fire is prepared, not that it is a threat invented to win an argument. Its reality answers the reality of the choice, and its readiness removes the comfort of endless delay. A later warning to believers also speaks of (66:6 — **“a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, overseen by formidable and severe angels”**). Thus the present verse should not feed pride in a person who confesses faith. It should guard faith from denial and guard the household from a road toward ruin. Today, the challenge and warning still stand side by side: examine the claim honestly, accept the verdict of the evidence, and let fear perform its proper work before the prepared end is seen.

---

## Verse 2:25

> Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those who believe and do good that they will have Gardens under which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,” for they will be served fruit that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses, and they will be there forever

**GOOD NEWS ANSWERS THE WARNING WITHOUT WEAKENING IT**

The Fire in the last verse does not fill the whole view. God then commands, ***“Give good news ˹O Prophet˺ to those”*** ***“who believe and do good”***. Fear shows a road to ruin, while good news gives the heart a home to seek. The Prophet must announce that home before his hearers can see it. Faith receives the promise as true. Good deeds show that faith has begun to guide the body, wealth, speech, and daily choices. This is why the two belong together rather than competing for the same place. Deeds do not buy Paradise at a price equal to it, for lasting bliss is a gift far beyond a person’s work. Yet inward belief is not an excuse for a barren life. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the good works as acts of obedience that bind servants to their Lord. Such acts make the outer life agree with the heart. This is the opposite of the split just exposed in the hypocrites. Their words and aims pulled apart; here trust and action meet. The same pair appears in the promise, (18:107 — **“Indeed, those who believe and do good will have the Gardens of Paradise as an accommodation”**). This matters because Quranic hope is not a wish that leaves conduct untouched. It is news believed so firmly that a person starts walking toward its truth now.

**THE GARDEN IS A HOME OF LIFE, NOT A THIN IDEA**

The news is ***“that they will have Gardens under”*** ***“which rivers flow. Whenever provided with fruit, they will say, “This is what we were given before,””***. The plural presents plenty rather than one small plot. Running water adds life, ease, beauty, and a sure supply. “Under” need not mean that the water is hidden beneath the soil. Early readings place the rivers below the trees and homes, or flowing through the Gardens. This detail would speak with special force to people who knew dry land and rare surface water. The point is that the waters belong to the Garden’s visible life and ease, not that they must be buried from view. Ibn ʿAbbās names rivers of water, milk, honey, and wine. A fuller description mentions (47:15 — **“that never changes in taste, rivers of wine delicious to drink,”**). The picture should not be emptied into a mere symbol, as if bodily joy were too low for God to give. Yet earthly life does not set the limit of what Paradise can be. Familiar words give a true promise that people can grasp, while its final form is greater than present thought. A flowing river in dry country can mean relief, safety, food, and rest at once. The Garden holds all these goods without dirt, fear, unfair control, or loss. God does not promise bare life after judgment. He promises a home where each sign of life comes from a Giver whose care never runs out.

**RESEMBLANCE MAKES EACH GIFT BOTH WELCOME AND NEW**

The residents remember an earlier gift, ***“for they will be served fruit”*** ***“that looks similar ˹but tastes different˺. They will have pure spouses”***. Early readers gave two main senses to “before.” It may recall fruit known in this world, or an earlier serving within Paradise. Both readings join recognition to fresh wonder. The difference between the readings is the remembered setting, not the promise that each new gift surpasses what was known. The fruit looks known in colour, shape, or kind, yet its taste is new. Ibn ʿAbbās explains the likeness through the same appearance with a different taste. The person can therefore welcome what is offered without already knowing all that it will give. Paradise avoids two limits of earthly pleasure. It is neither strange in a way that keeps joy at a distance nor repeated in a way that wears joy out. The gift can be known and still surprise. Its fruit is also (56:33 — **“never out of season nor forbidden—”**). No one waits in fear for the crop to fail. No owner locks the best part away. No last piece brings the good season to an end. This promise can train gratitude now. Common mercies often become hard to see because their names repeat: water, bread, shelter, a friend, another morning. Yet a repeated kind is not the same gift. It comes in a new hour, meets a present need, and gives one more chance to know and thank the Provider.

**PURITY AND PERMANENCE REMOVE THE SHADOW FROM JOY**

The promised companionship is pure. The words about spouses remove bodily filth, hurt, spite, betrayal, and each flaw that makes closeness unsafe. Early explanations mention freedom from menstruation and other impurity, but the broad promise is not confined to one bodily point. It presents a bond free from whatever spoils love or peace. The Quran also speaks of people entering (13:23 — **“the Gardens of Eternity, which they will enter along with the righteous among their parents, spouses,”**). Paradise is not a lonely feast or selfish desire cut loose from faithful ties. Its close bonds are healed under God’s pleasure. Then the last phrase makes every other gift secure: ***“and they will be there forever”***. A fine home can be darkened by the thought that it will decay. Love can ache under the fear of parting. Food ends, health fails, and every earthly stay must close. None of those shadows crosses this home. This is why forever changes the quality of every gift named before it, not just the length of the stay. Ibn ʿAbbās explains that its people neither die nor face exile. Another verse says, (15:48 — **“No fatigue will touch them there, nor will they ever be asked to leave”**). Life there does not grow stale. Weariness belongs to frail hearts and goods that lose their power to please. The Garden joins renewed gifts, clean hearts, and God’s endless grace. A brief good deed is not a poor exchange when the promised home never fades and never sends its people away.

---

## Verse 2:26

> Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito or what is even smaller. As for the believers, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?” Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray, and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious—

**NO TRUE LESSON IS TOO SMALL FOR DIVINE SPEECH**

The next words answer an objection about what God chooses to mention: ***“Surely Allah does not shy away from using the parable of a mosquito”***. Reports differ about the first objectors. Some connect their scorn to the fire and storm used for hypocrites. Others connect it to people who mocked the Qur’an for speaking of a fly or a spider. The shared fault is clear. They decide that a small creature is beneath divine speech, then treat their taste as a measure of God’s wisdom. Yet size does not decide whether an example is true. A fly can expose the weakness of an idol because all false gods together cannot make one: (22:73 — **“those ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah can never create ˹so much as˺ a fly, even if they ˹all˺ were to come together”**). A spider’s home can expose trust placed in powerless protectors: (29:41 — **“And the flimsiest of all shelters is certainly that of a spider, if only they knew”**). Qatādah says that God does not hold back from truth when He gives a parable, whether its subject seems great or small. The point is that divine majesty is not guarded by hiding the facts of creation. The smallest life may display power that human beings cannot give, and a plain image may uncover pride that grand speech leaves untouched.

**THE MOSQUITO MEASURES THE HEARER, NOT THE CREATOR**

The range remains open with ***“or what is even smaller.”*** The underlying expression was also read as what is above the mosquito in size, while another reading follows the sense used here: what goes still further in smallness. Neither makes the lesson depend on a fixed scale. If the truth needs a creature larger than a mosquito, that creature serves. If it needs one still less impressive to human eyes, smallness gives no ground for shame. This is why the mosquito tests judgment. A person may praise vast skies as signs, yet refuse to learn from a wing, a bite, or a fragile life near the skin. That refusal mistakes human notice for true worth. The mosquito is easy to dismiss but hard to create, complete with the parts and powers needed for its brief life. Ibn ʿAbbās presses this point: all created beings could join forces and still fail to create what the objector calls low. The difference between a useful parable and a poor one therefore lies in truth and fit, not in the social rank people give its subject. A teacher may use a grain, shadow, thread, or insect if it makes the matter clear. God knows the full reality of both the example and the thing shown by it. His choice lowers no truth; it lowers the pride that will only listen when the image flatters it.

**ONE PARABLE REVEALS TWO WAYS OF HEARING**

The first response is calm: ***“As for the believers, they know”*** ***“that it is the truth from their Lord.”*** They may not yet grasp every detail, but they know that the Lord does not speak without wisdom. That trust is not a ban on thought. It gives thought a sound start, so they attend to the point instead of inventing a flaw in the object used. People grounded in knowledge answer difficult revelation with, (3:7 — **“our Lord.” But none will be mindful ˹of this˺ except people of reason”**), after confessing that it all comes from Him. The second response exposes a different aim: ***“And as for the disbelievers, they argue, “What does Allah mean by such a parable?””*** The same words could form an honest question, but here the speakers use them to reject before learning. Their issue is not lack of an answer. It is scorn for the form in which the answer came. Therefore, the parable does more than carry an idea; it reveals whether the hearer seeks guidance or an excuse. The Quran later records almost the same taunt over the number of Hell’s keepers, then says the test causes believers to grow in faith. A reader should not fear a sincere question, since careful inquiry can serve belief. The danger begins when a question is made impossible to answer because its hidden rule is that God must first speak according to the hearer’s pride.

**GUIDANCE AND ERROR PART AT A MORAL FAULT LINE**

The result is stated as divine action: ***“Through this ˹test˺, He leaves many to stray”*** ***“and guides many. And He leaves none to stray except the rebellious”***. One revealed parable becomes guidance to some and a further step into error for others. This does not mean that the words are empty and each reader may make them mean anything. The truth remains one, but the moral response differs. Believers receive, think, and gain light. The rebellious resist, mock, and make their refusal harder. Thus the Quran can be (17:82 — **“a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss”**). The reason is not a defect in the medicine. A cure refused can become one more witness that the sick person chose against help. Nor does the verse portray error as a random trap laid for innocent seekers. It limits this leaving astray to the rebellious, and the next verse will name their breach, severing, and harm. A similar order appears when a people first choose a crooked course: (61:5 — **“when you already know I am Allah’s messenger to you?” So when they ˹persistently˺ deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”**). God’s judgment is real, and so is the revolt it judges. The safe response is not to demand a sign shaped by pride, but to ask what truth the given sign makes plain and then submit to the Lord who gave it.

---

## Verse 2:27

> those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption in the land. It is they who are the ˹true˺ losers

**REBELLION IS NOW SHOWN IN ITS BROKEN BONDS**

The “rebellious” at the end of verse 26 are not left as a vague class. They are ***“those who violate Allah’s covenant after it has been affirmed, break whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained”***. The first image is of something made firm and then undone. To violate a covenant is not simply to overlook an unknown duty. It is to treat a known bond as though it no longer binds. Early readings apply the covenant at several levels. It includes the basic claim of the Creator upon His creatures, God’s commands given through revelation, the pledges placed upon earlier communities, and the duty to receive a true messenger. These senses share one root: God has made His right known, and the rebel answers a settled claim with breach. The Quran recalls the first human witness when God asked, (7:172 — **“and had them testify regarding themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ “Am I not your Lord?” They replied, “Yes, You are!”**). It also records the covenant laid upon the prophets concerning a confirming messenger: (3:81 — **“if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.” He added,”**). The point is not to blur every covenant into one event. It is to show that revolt takes shape wherever a person receives a binding truth from God and then works to unmake its hold.

**AFFIRMATION MAKES THE LATER BREACH MORE GRAVE**

The reference to prior affirmation adds moral weight. A rope that was never tied cannot be accused of being untied. Here the bond was made firm by witness, promise, revealed command, clear proof, or all of these in their proper settings. This is why the breach is more than weakness during an honest search. The violator has enough ground to be bound and still chooses release from the duty. Ibn ʿAbbās applies the verse to the pledge concerning the Prophet: people had confirmed what bound them, then resisted the messenger named by that duty. Other early explanations widen the covenant to God’s charge that people obey His commands and avoid what He forbids. The readings meet rather than cancel one another. A covenant with God cannot be kept while His true message is rejected, and a verbal pledge is hollow when life refuses His rule. The opposite character appears in those (13:20 — **“who honour Allah’s covenant, never breaking the pledge”**). Honour here requires more than preserving the words of a promise. It means allowing the promise to govern the moment when keeping it becomes costly. Many pledges feel firm while nothing presses them. Their truth appears when status, desire, tribe, wealth, or fear pulls the other way. The verse therefore asks a living reader not only what was once affirmed, but which present choice is quietly trying to loosen it.

**WHAT GOD JOINS REACHES FROM WORSHIP TO HUMAN DUTY**

The second mark is severing what should remain joined. Ibn ʿAbbās includes sworn bonds and family ties, as well as the bond of faith with the Messenger. Other explanations extend the words to every relation God has ordered people to maintain: the servant with the Lord, children with parents, relatives with one another, neighbours, friends, believers, and human beings bound by justice. This breadth is sound because the phrase itself says “whatever” God ordered, not one tie alone. The Quran gives the positive mirror in those (13:21 — **“and those who maintain whatever ˹ties˺ Allah has ordered to be maintained, stand in awe of their Lord, and fear strict judgment”**). Joining begins with loyalty to God, since His command defines and protects the other bonds. It then becomes visible in care, truth, aid, lawful loyalty, and refusal to abandon a duty when a person is no longer useful. Family ties deserve clear stress, but they do not permit support for wrong. Nor does devotion to God excuse cruelty toward people. The same Lord commands both worship and justice. Therefore, the joined life is not a web of blind attachment. It is an ordered set of bonds kept under God. Sin cuts across that order: it separates claim from conduct, knowledge from obedience, kin from kin, and the good of one person from concern for another.

**CORRUPTION ENDS IN THE LOSS OF THE SELF**

Broken bonds do not remain private. Such people ***“and spread corruption in the land. It is they”*** ***“who are the ˹true˺ losers”***. Corruption includes blocking faith, weakening trust, spreading disobedience, and harming the relations on which common life rests. This is why another verse places public ruin and severed kinship in one line: (47:22 — **“Now if you ˹hypocrites˺ turn away, perhaps you would then spread corruption throughout the land and sever your ˹ties of˺ kinship”**). A person may imagine that breaking a pledge creates freedom or that cutting a demanding bond saves effort. The final account reverses that judgment. The rebel loses trust in this life, loses the good carried by faithful ties, and faces the loss of the Hereafter. Ibn ʿAbbās calls them cheated of both worlds. The strongest loss is not merely that some advantage slips away; the person has spent the self on a course that cannot deliver safety. Surah al-ʿAṣr begins with the rule (103:2 — **“Surely humanity is in ˹grave˺ loss”**) and then names the way out through faith, good work, truth, and patient counsel. Each of those repairs a bond this verse shows being cut. Thus the passage answers the taunt about a mosquito with a moral portrait. The parable did not force innocent people off the road. It exposed people already willing to break God’s claim, divide what He joined, and call the resulting damage gain.

---

## Verse 2:28

> How can you deny Allah? You were lifeless and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and again bring you to life, and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**THE QUESTION TURNS DENIAL TOWARD THE DENIER’S OWN LIFE**

The address changes from describing rebels to confronting them: ***“How can you deny Allah?”*** This is not a request for information about the method of disbelief. It is a rebuke filled with wonder. Denial cannot stand honestly when the denier’s own existence points beyond him. The verse does not begin with a remote object that only a trained observer can study. It begins with the hearer’s passage from no earthly life to life. A person may dispute a report, avoid a moral demand, or credit created means for present comfort. He still cannot claim to have called himself into being. The Quran presses the same fact through two short questions: (52:35 — **“Or were they created by nothing, or are they ˹their own˺ creators”**). Neither path can bear thought. Nothing has no will with which to make a person, and a person cannot create himself before he exists. Therefore, the question in this verse joins evidence to gratitude. The One who gave life has both the power to be known and the right to be thanked. Denial is strange not only because it rejects an argument, but because it uses a given mind, breath, and tongue against the Giver. Each moment of living is part of the evidence the question asks the hearer to face.

**THE FIRST GIFT CAME BEFORE ANY HUMAN CLAIM**

The first stage is plain: ***“You were lifeless and He gave you life”***. Early explanation takes the lifeless state as nonexistence, or as the lifeless material from which the body would be formed. Ibn ʿAbbās speaks of drops held in the bodies of fathers and then given life in the wombs of mothers. The readings meet in the fact that no human being possessed this worldly life and then granted it to himself. There was a time when each person was (76:1 — **“nothing yet worth mentioning”**). Then God brought hidden matter through stages into a living child who could sense, learn, choose, and answer. This is why life is a proof before it is an achievement. Parents are real causes, and the growth of the body follows an ordered process, but neither parents nor process invent the power of life. They work within a creation already given. The verse also checks pride. Wealth, education, family name, and skill all arrive after this first gift. None can become the ground for independence from God because each depends on the life He supplied before its owner could ask. A reader who has grown used to breathing may treat life as private property. These words return it to its true place: a received trust whose beginning was wholly beyond the receiver’s control.

**DEATH IS FOLLOWED BY A SECOND ACT OF LIFE**

The path does not stop at birth. God says, ***“then He will cause you to die”*** ***“and again bring you to life”***. Death comes when the appointed earthly term is complete. Its certainty strips present strength of any claim to permanence. Yet the verse places death between two acts of divine giving, not at the end of the line. The One who caused the first life is not weakened when that life closes. Resurrection is a new life for judgment, and the first creation is evidence that the second is within the same power. Ibn ʿAbbās reads the sequence as nonexistence, creation, death, and life on the Day of Resurrection. Another passage gives the same order in two brief statements: (23:15 — **“After that you will surely die”**) and (23:16 — **“then on the Day of Judgment you will be resurrected”**). The point is not that rebirth is a natural cycle that bodies produce on their own. It is an act of the Lord who first made them. When decayed bones are raised as an objection, the answer is, (36:79 — **“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “They will be revived by the One Who produced them the first time,”**). Death therefore humbles every human power without defeating hope. It ends the time for earthly work, while God’s power opens the life in which that work will be weighed.

**THE RETURN GIVES EVERY STAGE ITS MORAL END**

The sequence closes, ***“and then to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned”***. Return does not mean that human beings had escaped God’s knowledge or rule during life. It means that they are brought to the meeting, judgment, and repayment that no worldly shelter can delay. Early readers therefore connect the phrase with being repaid for one’s deeds. This is why the verse does more than prove that a Maker exists. It sets human freedom inside an account. The first life is received, the earthly term is limited, death is certain, the next life is real, and the final destination is God. Those stages leave no room for the idea that conduct vanishes when the body falls. On that Day some will admit, (40:11 — **“They will plead, “Our Lord! You made us lifeless twice, and gave us life twice. Now we confess our sins.”**). Their confession will be true but late. The present verse gives the same knowledge while repentance and good work remain possible. Today, people often plan as though birth were self-owned, death remote, and the future no more than memory left in others. The full line corrects that short view. Life is from God, death occurs by His decree, resurrection answers His promise, and return places every secret and public act before Him. Gratitude is therefore not only a feeling about being alive. It is to spend the entrusted life in readiness for the One who gave it and will call it back.

---

## Verse 2:29

> He is the One Who created everything in the earth for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens. And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**THE GIVER OF LIFE ALSO PREPARED A WORLD FOR IT**

The argument moves from the life of each person to the setting that sustains all people: ***“He is the One”*** ***“Who created everything in the earth”***. The One who brought a human being from lifelessness also made the soil, water, plants, animals, minerals, and countless links on which earthly life rests. This widens the proof in verse 28. A person did not create himself, and humanity as a whole did not create the field in which its work becomes possible. Farmers act, builders shape, doctors treat, and makers combine materials. None gives matter its first being or writes the laws by which it can be used. Ibn ʿAbbās points to beasts, plants, and other things as blessings made ready for benefit. The reference to the whole keeps gratitude from shrinking to a few obvious goods. A bitter plant may hold medicine, a hard rock may support a home, and a creature not eaten by people may serve an order that preserves their food. Some uses are known at once; others are found after long study. Therefore, the earth is both provision and sign. Another verse speaks of what God made on it in many colours and closes, (16:13 — **“for those who are mindful”**). Matter is not mute when its source, order, and service are read together.

**FOR YOU MEANS GIFT, USE, AND ACCOUNTABLE CARE**

The next words begin ***“for you. Then He turned towards the heaven, forming it into seven heavens.”*** Before the gaze rises, “for you” gives human beings permission to benefit from what is in the earth. Early legal reflection drew from this gift a broad starting rule of permitted and pure use, while excluding what God forbids and what causes harm. The phrase does not mean that every desire makes a use lawful. A gift remains under the will of its Giver. Nor does human benefit mean that no other creature has a claim within the earthly order. God also says, (55:10 — **“He laid out the earth for all beings”**). People may eat, build, travel, learn, and turn materials into useful goods, but they may not answer generosity with waste or ruin. The reason is that being served by creation makes gratitude more urgent, not ownership absolute. Elsewhere God says He subjected what lies in heaven and earth, then calls it (45:13 — **“by His grace. Surely in this are signs for people who reflect”**). Grace asks for thanks, and signs ask for thought. In daily life those two meet. Food should be received without pride, skill used without claiming self-creation, and natural wealth handled without forgetting those who come later. The earth is placed within human reach, but humanity still remains within God’s rule.

**SEVEN HEAVENS DISPLAY ORDER BEYOND THE HUMAN DWELLING**

The sentence then lifts attention from what is near to what rises above. The wording about God turning toward the heaven concerns His directing the act of creation and forming it as He willed. It does not require imagining created movement, bodily need, or effort in Him. Once He wills, no obstacle delays the result. The singular “heaven” is then formed into seven heavens, a complete ordered creation rather than an unshaped mass. Mujāhid describes the heavens as one above another, and another passage states that God formed them while assigning each its order: (41:12 — **“So He formed the heaven into seven heavens in two Days, assigning to each its mandate.”**). The number should be received as revealed truth, not reduced to a loose way of saying many. At the same time, the verse does not invite guesses that identify each heaven with any current human chart. Observation of the visible sky is good, but revelation speaks of a created order larger than what unaided sight can map. The point here is plain enough: the Lord who fitted the earth for life also formed the heights in ordered levels. This is why resurrection is no strain upon Him. The first making of the heavens and earth is greater than restoring one human body, yet both stand under the same command.

**PERFECT KNOWLEDGE HOLDS THE WHOLE AND EACH DETAIL**

The close is ***“And He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things”***. Power has not acted without wisdom, and the vastness of creation has not hidden one part from its Maker. His knowledge holds the earth and seven heavens as a whole, while missing no seed, creature, need, deed, or hidden thought within them. The question elsewhere makes the link direct: (67:14 — **“How could He not know His Own creation? For He ˹alone˺ is the Most Subtle, All-Aware”**). Human makers can lose track of what they make because their knowledge is partial and their control fades. God’s knowledge is not gained by trial, enlarged by discovery, or threatened by number.
